narrative:
The model estimates you have a 15% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Among students who passed, zero past failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees the complete lack of prior setbacks as a warning sign rather than a strength. 

The second strongest influence is your strong desire to pursue higher education. This works in your favor and pulls the prediction toward passing, which makes sense because every student who passed also wanted to continue studying.

Third, your low amount of free time after school also nudges the outcome toward passing. Most students who succeeded had medium or high free time, so your more limited free time is viewed by the model as a sign you may be focused on responsibilities rather than distractions.

To improve, you should look at two areas the model flagged indirectly: your study time is currently under two hours per week (lower than the 55% of successful students who study 2–5 hours), and you have had eight absences compared with an average of under four among those who passed. Increasing consistent study time and reducing absences are the most practical steps you can take to turn that 15% risk into a clear pass.
